# Distributions

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Descriptive statistics";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` tardigrades are animals about [0.5 mm]{.hl} long, with eight stubby legs. The German pastor J.A.E. Goeze first described them in 1773 and called them _kleiner Wasserbär_: "little water bear".

_Source: National Geographic_
:::

## Why describe?

A data set with 344 penguins is too much to take in at once. A [descriptive statistic]{.hl} summarises it in one number, such as a typical value or how much the values vary.

. . .

Like a map, a summary leaves most of the detail out. Today is about choosing a good summary, and noticing when it hides something important.

## Today

- What a distribution is: empirical and theoretical
- Measures of central tendency: mean, median, mode
- Measures of spread: standard deviation, MAD, range, quantiles
- When each map misleads: skew, outliers, more than one peak
- Grouped summaries and plots, building on `{dplyr}`

## Distributions

A [distribution]{.hl} shows how often each value, or range of values, occurs.

- An empirical distribution describes the values we actually observed
- A theoretical distribution is a mathematical shape, fully described by a few numbers called [parameters]{.hl}

. . .

We compare the two all the time: does our sample look like a shape we know?

## Plotting with `{ggplot2}` {.smaller}

Last week's promise: `{ggplot2}` builds a plot in layers, added with `+`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggplot(data, aes(x = column)) +   # the data, and which column goes where
  geom_histogram() +              # how to draw it
  labs(x = "Axis label")          # labels
```

- `ggplot()` and `aes()` say which data to use and which column goes on `x`, `y` or `colour`
- A `geom_*()` draws the shapes: `geom_histogram()`, `geom_point()`, `geom_boxplot()`
- `labs()` and `theme()` change the labels and the look

. . .

Our slides use a theme set up in the hidden first chunk of the .Rmd: your plots will look different, but show the same data.

## An empirical distribution {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "#5aa0e0", colour = "#0b110e") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Count")
```

Each bar counts the penguins whose flipper length falls in a 3 mm bin.

## Histogram or density? {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 3,
                 fill = "#5aa0e0", colour = "#0b110e", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density(colour = "#f2d45c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

The [density]{.hl} curve is a smoothed histogram. The area under it is 1.

## The normal distribution

In a [normal]{.hl} (or Gaussian) distribution, values are spread symmetrically around the mean, and most of them lie close to it: the familiar bell shape.

. . .

Two parameters describe it completely: the [mean]{.hl} and the [standard deviation]{.hl}.

. . .

```{r}
set.seed(42)    # same random numbers every time we knit
normal <- rnorm(500, mean = 0, sd = 1)
head(round(normal, 2))
```

## Sample vs theory {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 4.2}
tibble(value = normal) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "#e08ab8", colour = "#0b110e", alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, colour = "#f2d45c", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Density")
```

Bars: our 500 random values. Line: the [theoretical]{.hl} normal curve.

## The 68–95–99.7 rule

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
curve_df <- tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.01), y = dnorm(x))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(curve_df, abs(x) <= 3), fill = pandan, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_area(data = filter(curve_df, abs(x) <= 2), fill = pandan, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_area(data = filter(curve_df, abs(x) <= 1), fill = pandan, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_line(colour = mist, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.18, label = "68%", colour = floor_col,
           size = 7, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1.5, 1.5), y = 0.05, label = "95%", colour = mist, size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-2.5, 2.5), y = 0.012, label = "99.7%", colour = mist, size = 4.5,
           vjust = -1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3,
                     labels = c("-3 SD", "-2 SD", "-1 SD", "mean", "+1 SD", "+2 SD", "+3 SD")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density")
```

In a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.

## Other distributions {.smaller}

Not every variable is normal. Three shapes you will meet in linguistic data:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1)
discrete <- bind_rows(
  tibble(dist = "Binomial: correct out of 20",
         x = rbinom(1000, size = 20, prob = 0.85)),
  tibble(dist = "Poisson: pauses per minute",
         x = rpois(1000, lambda = 2.5))
)
continuous <- tibble(dist = "Log-normal: RTs (ms)",
                     x = rlnorm(1000, meanlog = log(600), sdlog = 0.3))

ggplot() +
  geom_bar(data = discrete, aes(x = x), fill = kingfisher, width = 0.8) +
  geom_histogram(data = continuous, aes(x = x), bins = 35,
                 fill = orchid, colour = floor_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ dist, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 13))
```

Accuracy out of a fixed number of trials is [binomial]{.hl} (lecture 12). Counts of events, such as pauses per minute, are often Poisson. Reaction times and durations are positive with a long right tail, closer to a log-normal or gamma shape.

# Central tendency

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a protein found only in tardigrades, Dsup, protects DNA from radiation. Human cells given the gene for it showed about [40% less DNA damage]{.hl} after X-rays.

_Source: Hashimoto et al. (2016), Nature Communications_
:::

## The tools of the trade

Descriptive measures come in two kinds:

| Central tendency | Spread |
|---|---|
| `mean()` | `sd()`, `var()` |
| `median()` | `mad()`, `IQR()` |
| mode | `range()`, `quantile()` |

. . .

Always report one of each: a measure of [centre]{.hl} and a measure of [spread]{.hl}.

## First: missing values {.smaller}

```{r}
mean(penguins$bill_length_mm)
mean(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

. . .

`NA` means "unknown". The mean of numbers that include an unknown is unknown, unless you tell R to drop them.

. . .

Three ways to drop missing values, three different data sets:

```{r}
nrow(penguins)                               # all rows
nrow(drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm))      # NA in bill length only
nrow(na.omit(penguins))                      # NA in any column
```

## `na.omit()` changes your result

```{r}
mean(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)   # 342 penguins
mean(na.omit(penguins)$bill_length_mm)        # 333 penguins
```

. . .

`na.omit()` also dropped 9 penguins with a known bill length but unknown `sex`.

. . .

Rule of thumb: drop `NA`s only in the columns you are analysing, with `na.rm = TRUE` or `drop_na(column)`.

## `mean()`

The mean is the sum of all values divided by their number

<div class="formula"><span style="text-decoration: overline;">x</span> = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) / n</div>

. . .

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
sum(x) / length(x)
mean(x)
```

## `mean()` {.smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_density(fill = pandan, colour = pandan, alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_mean, colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = bill_mean, y = 0.005, label = paste("mean =", round(bill_mean, 1)),
           fill = floor_col, colour = kingfisher, label.size = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

## `median()`

The [median]{.hl} is the middle value once all values are sorted from lowest to highest: half the values lie below it, half above.

. . .

```{r}
median(c(3, 1, 5))        # sorted: 1 3 5
median(c(3, 1, 5, 7))     # sorted: 1 3 5 7 -> mean of 3 and 5
```

. . .

With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

## `median()` {.smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_bill   = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_bill = median(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_density(fill = pandan, colour = pandan, alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_mean, colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_med, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("label", x = bill_mean, y = 0.005, label = "mean", hjust = 1.1,
           fill = floor_col, colour = kingfisher, label.size = 0, size = 5) +
  annotate("label", x = bill_med, y = 0.005, label = "median", hjust = -0.1,
           fill = floor_col, colour = hornbill, label.size = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

## One number can hide a lot

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm), aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_density(aes(fill = species, colour = species), alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_density(colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_mean, colour = mist, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Density", fill = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

The overall mean (`r round(bill_mean, 1)` mm) sits in a dip: few penguins actually have a bill that long. The distribution has three species in it.

## Skewed data: reaction times

Reaction times cannot be negative, and some responses are very slow:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
rt <- tibble(rt = rlnorm(2000, meanlog = log(600), sdlog = 0.35))
rt |> summarise(mean = mean(rt), median = median(rt))
```

## Skewed data: reaction times

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(rt, aes(x = rt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = orchid, colour = floor_col, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(rt$rt), colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(rt$rt), colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Reaction time (ms)", y = "Count")
```

A long right tail pulls the mean (dashed) away from the median (dotted).

## Outliers

One participant fell asleep on one trial:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
rts <- round(rlnorm(40, meanlog = log(600), sdlog = 0.25))
rts_sleepy <- c(rts, 5000)

tibble(data   = c("40 trials", "40 trials + one 5000 ms"),
       mean   = c(mean(rts), mean(rts_sleepy)),
       median = c(median(rts), median(rts_sleepy)))
```

. . .

The mean moves by more than 100 ms. The median barely moves: it is [robust]{.hl}.

## Discussion

Here we know that the participant fell asleep. In real data, a 5,000 ms response usually comes with no explanation.

- Would you remove it? How would you decide which responses are too slow?
- Why does it matter whether you decide before or after looking at the results?

## Mode {.smaller}

The mode is the most frequent value. It is used in __categorical__ distributions.

. . .

With `count()` from last week:

```{r}
penguins |> count(island) |> slice_max(n)
```

. . .

```{r}
words <- tibble(word = c("the", "cat", "saw", "the", "dog", "and", "the", "bird"))
words |> count(word, sort = TRUE) |> head(3)
```

## Mode: a trap {.smaller}

R has a function called `mode()`, but it does not compute the mode:

```{r}
mode(c("Hello", "Hello", "Goodbye"))
```

. . .

It returns the storage type. If you need a function, write your own:

```{r}
find_mode <- function(x) {
  u <- unique(x)
  tab <- tabulate(match(x, u))
  u[tab == max(tab)]
}
find_mode(c("Hello", "Hello", "Goodbye", "Hello", "Penguin", "Dog", "Mountain"))
```

# Spread

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` when their home dries out, tardigrades lose their body water, curl up and enter [cryptobiosis]{.hl}, a deep sleep. They can revive years later, when water returns.

_Sources: National Geographic; ScienceDaily_
:::

## Same centre, different spread

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(11)
two_groups <- tibble(
  group = rep(c("Speaker A: SD = 20 ms", "Speaker B: SD = 60 ms"), each = 1000),
  duration = c(rnorm(1000, 150, 20), rnorm(1000, 150, 60))
)
ggplot(two_groups, aes(x = duration, fill = group, colour = group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 150, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Vowel duration (ms)", y = "Density", fill = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

Both speakers have a mean of 150 ms. Speaker B is far less consistent.

## `sd()`

The [standard deviation]{.hl} measures how spread out the values are around the mean: roughly, how far a typical value is from it.

<div class="formula">s = √( Σ (xᵢ − <span style="text-decoration: overline;">x</span>)² / (n − 1) )</div>

. . .

```{r}
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
sqrt(sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (length(x) - 1))
sd(x)
var(x)       # the variance is the SD squared
```

## `sd()` {.smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_bill   = sd(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.4}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = bill_mean - bill_sd, xmax = bill_mean + bill_sd,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = kingfisher, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_density(fill = pandan, colour = pandan, alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_mean, colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = bill_mean, y = 0.005, label = "mean ± 1 SD",
           fill = floor_col, colour = kingfisher, label.size = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

## `mad()`

The [median absolute deviation]{.hl} (MAD) is the robust partner of the SD: the median distance of the values from their median.

. . .

| Step | Values | |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1. The data, sorted | 1, 1, 2, __2__, 4, 6, 9 | median = 2 |
| 2. Distance of each value from 2 | 1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 4, 7 | |
| 3. The same distances, sorted | 0, 0, 1, __1__, 2, 4, 7 | MAD = 1 |

## `mad()` in R {.smaller}

```{r}
x <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 6, 9)
mad(x, constant = 1)
mad(x)
```

. . .

By default, `mad()` multiplies the result by 1.4826. With normal data, this makes the MAD estimate the SD, so the two are comparable.

. . .

```{r}
c(sd = sd(rts), mad = mad(rts))                    # 40 trials
c(sd = sd(rts_sleepy), mad = mad(rts_sleepy))      # + one 5000 ms trial
```

## `mad()` {.smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(median_bill = median(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            mad_bill    = mad(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = bill_med - bill_mad, xmax = bill_med + bill_mad,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = hornbill, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_density(fill = pandan, colour = pandan, alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bill_med, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("label", x = bill_med, y = 0.005, label = "median ± 1 MAD",
           fill = floor_col, colour = hornbill, label.size = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Density")
```

## `range()`

`range()` returns the smallest and the largest value. The distance between them is what statisticians call the range.

. . .

```{r}
range(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
diff(range(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

. . .

The range depends on two values only, the most extreme ones. One outlier changes it completely.

## Quantiles / Quartiles

[Quantiles]{.hl} cut the sorted values into groups of equal size. Quartiles cut them into four quarters:

```{r}
quantile(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)     # 75% minus 25%
```

. . .

The [median]{.hl} is the 50% quantile. The [IQR]{.hl} holds the middle half of the data.

## `summary()`

Most of today in one line:

```{r}
summary(penguins$bill_length_mm)
```

. . .

It works on a whole data frame too: try `summary(penguins)`.

## Boxplots draw the quartiles

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm),
       aes(x = species, y = bill_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.9, width = 0.5, colour = mist) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bill length (mm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Box: 25% to 75% (the IQR). Line: the median. Whiskers: to the furthest point within 1.5 × IQR of the box. Dots: every penguin.

# `group_by` and `summarise`

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in 2007, dried tardigrades flew into orbit on the FOTON-M3 mission and were exposed to [open space]{.hl}: vacuum, cosmic rays and solar UV over 1,000 times stronger than on Earth. Most survived the vacuum, a few even the full UV, and the survivors reproduced normally.

_Sources: Jönsson et al. (2008), Current Biology; ScienceDaily_
:::

## Summaries per group {.smaller}

Until now, we have summarised one distribution at a time.

. . .

Usually we want the same summary for each group: `bill_length_mm` for each species separately.

. . .

The bad way to do it:

```{r}
Adelie    <- filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
Gentoo    <- filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
Chinstrap <- filter(penguins, species == "Chinstrap")
mean(Adelie$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(Gentoo$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(Chinstrap$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## The good way {.smaller}

Last week: `group_by()` + `summarise()`, or `summarise(.by = )`

```{r}
penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarise(n      = n(),
            mean   = mean(bill_length_mm),
            sd     = sd(bill_length_mm),
            median = median(bill_length_mm),
            IQR    = IQR(bill_length_mm),
            .by    = species)
```

. . .

One row per species, one column per summary, no copies of the data.

## Grouping by two variables {.smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  drop_na(sex) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(mean_bill = mean(bill_length_mm),
            median_bill = median(bill_length_mm))
```

. . .

The message: the result is still grouped by species. Either add `.groups = "drop"`, `ungroup()` it, or use `.by = c(species, sex)`, which never leaves groups behind.

## `group_by()` or `.by`?

Use `group_by()` when several steps in a row should work per group, and `ungroup()` when you are done, before you save the result.

. . .

Use `.by` when only one step needs the groups. Nothing stays grouped afterwards, so there is nothing to forget.

## Many columns at once: `across()` {.smaller}

From last week: `across(columns, function)`

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(across(ends_with("_mm"),
                   list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                        sd   = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))),
            .by = species) |>
  select(species, starts_with("bill_length"))
```

. . .

`list(mean = ..., sd = ...)` applies two functions to each column, and adds `_mean` and `_sd` to the names.

## Plotting group summaries {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
bill_summary <- penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(bill_length_mm), sd = sd(bill_length_mm), .by = species)

ggplot(drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm), aes(x = species, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = species), width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_pointrange(data = bill_summary, colour = "#e3e8e1", linewidth = 1, size = 0.8,
                  aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bill length (mm)") + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Points: every penguin. White: mean ± 1 SD per species.

## Reporting descriptives {.smaller}

In R Markdown, numbers in your text can come straight from R:

```{r}
gentoo <- filter(bill_summary, species == "Gentoo")
```

```markdown
Gentoo bills were `r '\x60r round(gentoo$mean, 1)\x60'` mm long on average
(SD = `r '\x60r round(gentoo$sd, 1)\x60'`).
```

. . .

becomes

> Gentoo bills were `r round(gentoo$mean, 1)` mm long on average (SD = `r round(gentoo$sd, 1)`).

. . .

If the data change, the text updates itself, so you never copy numbers by hand.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- A summary is a simplified map of a distribution
- Centre: `mean()` (sensitive), `median()` (robust), mode with `count()`
- Spread: `sd()` (sensitive), `mad()` and `IQR()` (robust), `range()`, `quantile()`
- Always plot the data: skew, outliers and several peaks hide behind one number
- Per group: `summarise()` with `.by` or `group_by()`; many columns with `across()`
:::
